A rebuff is a rejection — but not just any ordinary rejection. It is a sharp, cold, and blunt refusal given to someone who has tried to reach out, connect, offer something, or get closer to you. What makes a rebuff different from a simple "no" is the manner in which it is delivered. It is dismissive. It is abrupt. It shuts the other person down — often leaving them feeling embarrassed, hurt, or discouraged.

A helpful way to hold onto this word: think of "buff" as in polishing something — making it welcome and smooth. A re*buff does the opposite. It pushes something away, roughens the interaction, and sends a clear signal: *not welcome here.
The Three Ingredients of a Rebuff

Every rebuff involves three things working together:

Someone makes an approach — they offer help, express interest, make a request, or try to be friendly. The other person turns that approach away — not kindly, but coldly and abruptly. And the person who was turned away is left stinging from the experience.

Remove any one of these elements and it's not quite a rebuff anymore. A gentle "no, thank you" is just a polite refusal. What makes a rebuff a rebuff is the coldness, the bluntness, and the sting it leaves behind.
Everyday Situations Where a Rebuff Happens

In personal life. Suppose you try to comfort a grieving friend, and they snap at you to leave them alone. That cold push-away is a rebuff. Or imagine someone working up the courage to tell a person they like them romantically, only to be met with silence and a look of disdain. That painful shut-down is a rebuff.

In professional life. A salesperson pitches their product to a company, and the executive cuts them off mid-sentence and walks out. That is a professional rebuff. An employee suggests a new idea in a meeting, and the manager dismisses it without even listening. That dismissal is a rebuff too.

In politics and diplomacy. A country reaches out to another to begin peace talks, and the other country publicly and coldly refuses. Journalists would almost certainly call that a diplomatic rebuff. A politician attempts to form an alliance with a rival party, only to be flatly turned down — that, too, is a rebuff.
What a Rebuff Feels Like (The Emotional Weight)

This is important, because a rebuff is not an emotionally neutral word. It carries a sting. The person who receives a rebuff almost always feels some combination of embarrassment, rejection, discouragement, or wounded pride. They put themselves out there — they took a risk — and they were shot down coldly.

This is why writers and speakers choose the word "rebuff" over a plain word like "refusal." "Refusal" is neutral. "Rebuff" tells you the rejection landed hard. It paints a fuller picture of what the experience felt like.
How Rebuff Is Used in Sentences

Notice how naturally it slots into different situations:

  • "She tried to apologize, but her gesture was met with a sharp rebuff."
  • "After yet another rebuff from publishers, he began to doubt his writing."
  • "The ambassador's peace overture suffered a humiliating rebuff."
  • "His attempts at friendship were greeted with constant rebuffs."
  • "She had grown used to rebuffs, but this one still hurt."

You'll notice rebuff is often paired with adjectives like sharp, cold, stinging, humiliating, or painful. These adjectives reinforce the idea of a rejection that doesn't just say no — it says no in a way that cuts.
How Rebuff Compares to Similar Words

Rejection is the closest word, but it is emotionally neutral. If a university doesn't accept your application, that's a rejection — it doesn't necessarily feel cold or personal. A rebuff is a rejection with teeth — delivered in a way that feels dismissive or unkind.

Snub is also similar. A snub is when someone deliberately ignores you or treats you as beneath their notice — like a celebrity walking past a fan without acknowledgment. A rebuff is more active: someone reaches out, and the other person actively and coldly turns them away. Both sting, but a snub is more about being ignored, while a rebuff is more about being pushed away.

Brush-off is an informal version of the same idea. "She gave him the brush-off" means the same thing as "she gave him a rebuff," but it's more casual and conversational. Rebuff is the more formal, literary choice.

Setback is completely different — it means an obstacle or a step backward in progress. Don't confuse them.

Rebuffs are not all equal. A mild rebuff is a firm but cold "no" that still feels unwelcoming. A sharp rebuff is blunt and possibly rude — it makes the other person feel foolish for even trying. A stinging or humiliating rebuff is one that publicly or deeply embarrasses the person who reached out.

The word rebuff, on its own, already implies some degree of coldness. But the adjective you pair it with tells you just how bad it was.

If you ever want to check whether "rebuff" is the right word, ask yourself: Did someone try to reach out, and were they turned away in a way that was cold, blunt, or dismissive — leaving them feeling pushed away or embarrassed? If yes, rebuff fits perfectly.
